system:
You read a video channel's mechanism references and decide whether they carry a move no technique covers.
A technique is a kind of motion graphic the designer is shown one finished example of. The catalogue
lists the house techniques; the channel may also have techniques of its own. Each mechanism reference
names, in its carry-over line and its reading, a move the owner wants borrowed as grammar.
If every move the references carry is already covered by a technique in the catalogue or among the
channel's own, answer {"proposal": null, "why": "..."} and say which technique covers each move.
Otherwise propose one technique, the one the references ask for most clearly, as JSON with the keys in this order:
{"proposal": {"key": "...", "name": "...", "description": "...", "steerPhrases": ["..."], "mechanisms": ["..."], "slot": {"durationMs": 6000, "words": [{"text": "...", "atMs": 0}], "intent": "..."}, "fromReference": "..."}, "why": "..."}
- "key": lower-case words joined by hyphens, under 40 characters, not a key in the catalogue or among the channel's own.
- "name": the technique in words, under 40 characters.
- "description": one line under 160 characters saying what the graphic does, as the catalogue describes its techniques.
- "steerPhrases": one to 4 phrases of two to four plain words a producer would type to ask for this technique, naming the move and not any house technique; no single words.
- "mechanisms": one to 6 keys from the list, the moves the design is built on.
- "slot": a synthetic slot for the channel's own example: 3 to 12 seconds, its narration as words on the clock in order and inside the slot, in this channel's register, and the intent the viewer must take away.
- "fromReference": the title of the reference the move came from.
- "why": under 600 characters: the move, where it was seen, and why no technique covers it.
A reference is grammar to learn from, never content to copy. Use no dash characters.

messages.content:
This channel's motion:
- The curves are soft (arrivals settle long, moves ease both ways).
- Things arrive by rise; overshoot: hair.
- Lengths in milliseconds: micro 120, enter 450, exit 300, reveal 550, draw 700, count 1000, move 900, gap 120.
- Something changes about every 1.5 seconds, and the camera never stops: a slow push over the whole slot (a scale of 2 to 4% on motion.ease.move), anchored at the content's edge or centre so nothing is pushed out of the safe area.
- Blur follows speed: an element moving fast takes a filter: blur() worked out from how far
  it moved since the frame before (compute its place at frame - 1), and none at rest.
- 3D when it carries meaning: perspective with rotateX or rotateY for a drum, a turn or a
  card, never a spin for its own sake.
- Charts stay honest and conventional: bars rise out of the baseline, lines draw on, a ring
  sweeps; no gridlines or minor ticks, and no bar that travels or morphs from one value to
  the next. The invention goes into the type, the framing and the hand-offs, never the data
  marks.
- Never: glows, particle bursts, lens flares, camera shake, RGB split, a crossfade from one whole layout to another, decorative gradients, drop shadows for depth.
- Nothing may stay still longer than 6 seconds.
Dark, slow, one figure at a time.

The channel's style guide:
Dark, slow, one figure at a time.

The mechanisms, by key: persistent-actor, foreground-becomes-transition, cause-to-effect, density-from-hierarchy, change-of-speed, hard-cut, word-splits-open, docking, drum, reel, draw-on, rise-from-baseline, tally, door, marker-stroke, camera-push.

The catalogue:
- stat-counter: the sentence parts and one large figure rises out of it, counting to its mark as the rule beneath it fills (built on word splits open, drum, draw on)
- kpi-counter: each figure lands large and counts, then docks into a row above as the next is introduced, the last left large (built on drum, docking, cause to effect)
- bar-chart: bars rising out of the baseline as their years are spoken, the last in the accent, then a line across the tops (built on rise from baseline, draw on)
- line-chart: a line drawn year by year with the ground under it filling behind the pen, the last value landing large beside its point (built on draw on, docking)
- racing-chart: horizontal bars that grow and overtake as the years are read, the year rolling on like a reel, the leader lit at the close (built on reel, rise from baseline, persistent actor)
- comparison-chart: two series rising side by side per year, the gap drawn as an empty outline on top of the shorter bar (built on rise from baseline, draw on)
- donut-chart: a ring that sweeps to a percentage as the figure inside counts, the slice pulling out when the narration says it went (built on draw on, drum, cause to effect)
- progress-bars: labelled bars filling to their share on equal tracks, one after another, the largest share on the hero spring (built on draw on, tally)
- progress-steps: steps lit in turn along a line drawn from one to the next, the walked steps stepping back, the last in the accent (built on draw on, tally, density from hierarchy)
- kinetic-word-stack: a repeated word built once and kept, what changes after it rolling past on a 3D drum, the last in the accent (built on persistent actor, drum, density from hierarchy)
- typewriter: a line typed out word by word as it is spoken, then swept with a selection as if about to be acted on (built on draw on, marker stroke)
- text-highlight: one phrase marked with a single unbroken stroke as it is said, the rest of the sentence stepping back (built on marker stroke, density from hierarchy)
- quote-card: a large opening mark that settles into the margin as the quotation builds, the attribution drawn off it by a rule (built on foreground becomes transition, draw on)
- animated-list: items entering one at a time beside a single marker that travels down to each, the earlier items stepping back (built on tally, persistent actor, density from hierarchy)
- lower-third: an accent bar that stands up first, the name sliding out from behind it and the role building on a widening band (built on door, cause to effect)
- chapter-title: the chapter label over a rule that draws out to the title's width, the title words dropping out from under it (built on draw on, cause to effect)
- logo-reveal: a lockup behind a pair of doors that slide apart as the name is said, its tracking settling, the line beneath (built on door, docking)
- split-screen: one claim centred, then the pivot word lands and collapses into the divider that splits the frame for the second (built on foreground becomes transition, word splits open, cause to effect)

The channel has no techniques of its own yet.

The mechanism references, by their readings:

Reference 1: "Ledger scene" (mechanism). Carry over: the ruled line that wipes the old figure away.
Medium: flat typography over paper
Palette: #111, #eee
Type: grotesk, heavy
Enters: written in
Exits: wiped by a rule
Motion: one line travels and the figure behind it changes
Absent: no glow, no particles

Decide, and answer.
